title: Of three good women
paragraphs: They are not by the dozen, as everyone knows, and especially in the duties of marriage; for marriage is a bargain full of so many delicate clauses that it is hard for a woman's will to bear that restraint for long. Men, though their condition is somewhat better under the same tie, still have enough on their hands. The true test of a happy marriage looks at the time of the companionship: whether it has been steadily gentle, loyal, and agreeable. In our day women commonly hold back the public showing of their good offices, and of their passionate affection for their husbands, until they have lost them — or at least put off the testimonies of their goodwill till then. A slow and untimely testimony. By it they rather demonstrate that they never loved their husbands until they were dead: their life is nothing but trouble, their death full of love and politeness. As fathers conceal their affection from their children, women conceal theirs from their husbands, to maintain a modest decorum. This kind of mystery is not to my taste. They scratch themselves and tear their hair for nothing. I whisper in a waiting-woman's or a secretary's ear: "How were they together, how did they live?" I always have that good saying in my head:
["They make the greatest show of grief who feel it least." — Tacitus, Annals, ii. 77, writing of Germanicus.]

Their wailing is offensive to the living and useless to the dead. We would willingly let them laugh once we are gone, provided they smile on us while we are alive. Is it not enough to make a man revive in pure spite — that she who spat in my face while I was alive should come and kiss my feet once I am dead? If there is any honour in mourning a husband, it belongs only to those who smiled on them while they had them; let those who wept during their lives laugh at their deaths, outwardly as well as inwardly. So never mind the puffy red eyes and the pitiful voice; look at her bearing, her colour, the plumpness of her cheeks under all those formal veils — that is where she speaks plain French. There are few who do not improve on it, and good health cannot lie. That starched and ceremonious expression looks not so much back as forward, and is meant rather to find a new husband than to mourn the old. When I was a boy, a very beautiful and virtuous lady, who is still alive, the widow of a prince, wore a little more ornament in her dress than our laws of widowhood allow; when she was reproached for it she answered that it was because she was resolved never again to have any love affair, and would never marry again.

I have here, not at all in opposition to our customs, picked out three women who likewise showed the utmost goodness and affection at the deaths of their husbands; but they are examples of a kind no longer in use, and so severe that they will hardly be drawn into imitation.

The younger Pliny had near a house of his in Italy a neighbour who was being tormented by certain ulcers on his private parts. His wife, seeing him drag on so long, asked him to let her examine the state of his disease at leisure, and to tell him frankly what she thought. He gave permission, and she, having looked carefully into the matter, found it impossible he could ever be cured: all he had to hope for was a long lingering, painful and miserable life. So, as the most sure and sovereign remedy, she calmly advised him to kill himself. But finding him a little tender and reluctant in so harsh an undertaking, she said, "Do not think, my dear, that the torments I see you in are not as keenly felt by me as by you, and that to deliver myself from them I will not myself use the same remedy I have prescribed for you. I will keep you company in the cure as I have done in the disease. Fear nothing — believe that we shall take pleasure in this passage, which is to free us from so many miseries; and we will go together happily." Having said that, and put fresh courage into her husband, she resolved that they should throw themselves headlong into the sea from a window that overlooked it. And so as to keep up to the last the loyal and passionate affection with which she had embraced him in his life, she wanted him to die in her arms as well — but lest they should let go of each other in the fall from fear, she bound herself fast to him at the waist, and so gave her own life to procure her husband's rest. This was a woman of low condition; and among that class of people it is no very new thing to see examples of rare virtue:
"Extrema per illos Justitia excedens terris vestigia fecit."
["Justice, when she left the earth, took her last steps among them." — Virgil, Georgics, ii. 473.]
The other two were noble and rich, and examples of virtue are seldom lodged there.

Arria, the wife of Caecina Paetus, a man of consular rank, was the mother of another Arria, the wife of Thrasea Paetus — the same Thrasea whose virtue was so celebrated in Nero's time — and through this son-in-law she was the grandmother of Fannia (the resemblance of these men's and women's names, and of their fortunes, has led to several confusions). This first Arria, when her husband Caecina Paetus had been captured by some of the Emperor Claudius' men after the defeat of Scribonianus — whose party he had embraced in the war — begged those who were to carry him prisoner to Rome to take her along on their ship, where she would be much less expense and trouble to them than the many attendants they would otherwise have to maintain to wait on her husband, and that she alone would undertake to look after him in his room, his kitchen, and every other office. They refused. So she put herself into a fisherman's boat she hired on the spot, and in that way followed him from Illyria. After her arrival at Rome, Junia, the widow of Scribonianus, one day, on the strength of their similar fortunes, came up to her in the Emperor's presence; Arria pushed her off roughly with these words: "I," she said, "speak to you, or listen to anything you have to say! — to you, in whose lap Scribonianus was killed, and you are still alive?" These words, with several other signs, made her friends realise she would certainly take her own life, unable to endure her husband's misfortune. And Thrasea, her son-in-law, begging her not to throw herself away, and saying to her, "What — if I should suffer the same fate as Caecina, would you want your daughter, my wife, to do the same?" — "Would I?" she replied. "Yes, yes, I would: if she had lived as long, and in as good understanding with you, as I have lived with my husband." These answers made them all the more careful of her, and more watchful in their eye on her. One day, when she said to those guarding her, "You take all this trouble for nothing; you may indeed make me die a worse death, but to keep me from dying is not in your power" — she suddenly leapt from a chair where she had been sitting and with all her strength dashed her head against the wall, by which blow she was knocked flat in a faint and badly wounded. After they had with great difficulty brought her back to herself, she said, "I told you that if you denied me some easy way of dying, I would find another, however painful." The conclusion of so admirable a virtue was this. Her husband Paetus, not having resolution enough of his own to despatch himself as the emperor's cruelty had ordered him to, one day, after she had used all the reasons and exhortations she thought most likely to persuade him, she snatched the dagger he wore at his side, held it ready in her hand to clinch her admonitions, and saying "Do this, Paetus," in the same instant gave herself a mortal stab in the breast, then drew it out of the wound and presented it to him, ending her life with this noble, generous, and immortal saying — "Paete, non dolet" — having time to pronounce no more than those three never-to-be-forgotten words: "Paetus, it does not hurt."
"Casta suo gladium cum traderet Arria Paeto, Quem de visceribus traxerat ipsa suis Si qua fides, vulnus quod feci non dolet, inquit, Sed quod tu facies, id mihi, Paete, dolet."

["When the chaste Arria gave to Paetus the reeking sword she had drawn from her own breast, 'If you believe me,' she said, 'Paetus, the wound I have made does not hurt; it is the one you will make, Paetus, that hurts me.'" — Martial, i. 14.]

The action was nobler in itself, and of a braver sense, than the poet expressed it. So far from being deterred by the thought of her husband's wound, his death, and her own, she had been the one to propose them and urge them; but having performed this high and courageous undertaking solely for her husband's sake, she was thinking, even in the last gasp of her life, only of him — of relieving him of the fear of dying along with her. Paetus at once stabbed himself to the heart with the same weapon, ashamed, I suppose, to have needed so dear and precious an example.

Pompeia Paulina, a young and very noble Roman lady, had married Seneca in his extreme old age. Nero, his fine pupil, sent his guards to him to deliver the death-sentence, which was carried out in this fashion: when the Roman emperors of those days had condemned a man of rank, they sent word by their officers to him to choose his manner of death, and to carry it out within such or such a time-limit, which was set, depending on the degree of their anger, either shorter or longer, so as to give him time to put his affairs in order — or sometimes to deny him even that, by the shortness of the period. If the condemned man seemed unwilling to obey the order, they had men ready to carry it out either by cutting the veins of his arms and legs, or by forcing him to swallow a dose of poison. But men of honour would not submit to that necessity, but called in their own doctors and surgeons for the job. Seneca, with a calm and steady face, heard their charge and at once called for paper to make his will. When the captain refused him this, he turned to his friends and said, "Since I am not allowed to leave you any other token of the debt I owe you, I leave you at least the best thing I have, namely the image of my life and conduct, which I beg you to keep in memory of me — and by doing so you will earn the glory of sincere and real friends." Then, one moment soothing with gentle words the grief he saw in them, the next raising his voice to rebuke them: "What," he said, "has become of all our fine philosophical maxims? What of all the provisions we have laid in for so many years against the strokes of fortune? Is Nero's cruelty unknown to us? What could we expect of one who has murdered his mother and his brother, but that he should put to death the tutor who brought him up?" After those general words, he turned to his wife and embraced her tightly in his arms, as, her heart and strength failing her, she was ready to sink down with grief; and he begged her, for his sake, to bear this stroke with a little more patience, telling her that the hour had come in which he was to show, not by argument and discourse but in action, the fruit he had reaped from his studies, and that he genuinely embraced his death, not only without grief but with joy. "And so, my dearest," he said, "do not dishonour it with your tears, lest it look as if you loved yourself more than my reputation. Restrain your grief, and console yourself in what you have known of me and of my actions, leading the rest of your life in the same virtuous way you have done up to now." Paulina, having recovered her spirits a little, and warmed the greatness of her courage with a most generous affection, replied: "No, Seneca, I am not a woman to let you go alone in such a moment. I will not have you think that the virtuous examples of your life have not taught me how to die; and when could I ever do it better, or more fittingly, or more as I would wish, than with you? So be sure: I will go along with you." Then Seneca, taking this noble and generous resolution of his wife in good part, and willing also to free himself from the fear of leaving her exposed to his enemies' cruelty after his death, said, "Paulina, I have instructed you in what would serve you for a happy life; but you, I see, are more set on the honour of dying. Truly, I will not grudge it to you. The steadiness and resolve in our common end are the same; but the beauty and glory of your part are much greater." That said, the surgeons at the same moment opened the veins of both their arms; but as Seneca's, more shrunken with age and abstinence, let his blood flow too slowly, he further ordered them to open the veins of his thighs. And so that the torments he was suffering might not pierce his wife's heart, and also to spare himself the affliction of seeing her in so sad a state, after a very affectionate farewell he begged her to allow them to carry her into her own room, which they did. But all these incisions still being not enough to make him die, he ordered Statius Annaeus, his physician, to give him a draught of poison, which had not much better effect — because of the weakness and coldness of his limbs it could not reach his heart. So they were forced to add a very hot bath; and then, feeling his end approach, while he still had breath he kept up admirable discourse on the subject of his present condition, which his secretaries took down as long as they could hear him; and his last words long remained in great honour and esteem among men, and it is a great loss to us that they have not come down to our day. Then, feeling the last pangs of death, with the bloody water of the bath he bathed his head and said, "This water I dedicate to Jupiter the Deliverer." Nero, hearing of all this at once, and fearing that the death of Paulina — who was one of the best-born ladies of Rome, and against whom he had no particular grudge — would turn into a reproach against him, sent orders in all haste to bind up her wounds. Her attendants did so without her knowledge, since she was already half dead and quite past all sensation. So although she lived against her own design, she lived very honourably, in a way befitting her own virtue, and her pale complexion afterwards bore continual witness to how much life had run out of her veins.

These are my three quite true stories, which I find as entertaining and as tragic as any of those we make up out of our own heads to amuse the common people. And I wonder why those who give themselves to such writing do not rather pick out ten thousand very fine stories which are to be found in books, which would save them the trouble of invention, and would be more useful and entertaining. Anyone who wanted to put a whole, connected body of them together would need to add nothing of his own but the joining — the solder of another metal, as it were — and might in that way assemble a great many true events of every kind, ordering and varying them according as the beauty of the work required, much as Ovid has built his Metamorphoses out of the endless number of his various fables.

In the last pair, there is moreover this to consider: that Paulina voluntarily offered to lose her life out of love of her husband, and that her husband had earlier refrained from dying out of love of her. We may think there is no fair counterbalance in this exchange; but, in his Stoic way, I take it he thought he had done as much for her by prolonging his life on her account as if he had died for her. In one of his letters to Lucilius, after letting him know that, struck down by a fever in Rome, he had at once taken his coach to head for a house of his in the country, against his wife's wish, who wanted him to stay — and that he had told her the fever he was struck with was not a fever of the body but of the place — he goes on: "She let me go," he says, "with strict orders to look after my health. Now I, knowing that her life is bound up in mine, am beginning to make much of myself, so that I can preserve her. And I lose the privilege my age has given me of being more steady and resolute in many things, when I remember that in this old fellow there is a young girl whose interests are tied to his health. And since I cannot persuade her to love me more bravely, she makes me love myself more solicitously. We must allow something to honourable affections; sometimes, even when occasions urge us the other way, we must call life back, even with pain; we must hold the soul fast in our teeth, since the rule of life for good men is not as long as they please but as long as they should. He who does not love his wife or his friend enough to prolong his life for them, but is set on dying, is too dainty and too soft. The soul must lay this duty on itself, when our friends' need requires it; we must sometimes lend ourselves to our friends, and break our resolve to die for ourselves on their behalf. It is a mark of greatness of courage to come back to life out of consideration for another, as many excellent men have done; and it is a mark of singular good nature to preserve old age — of which the chief convenience is indifference to its length and a stout, disdainful use of life — when a man sees that doing so is pleasant, agreeable, and useful to someone who loves him very much. And one reaps a very pleasing reward in it; for what can be more delightful than to be so dear to one's wife that on her account one becomes dearer to oneself? So my Paulina has loaded me not only with her fears but with my own; it has not been enough for me to consider how resolutely I could die — I have also had to consider how irresolutely she would bear my death. I am compelled to live, and sometimes to live in greatness of spirit." These are his own words, as excellent as they everywhere are.
